interest: This file offers valuable historical insight into the shifting legal and economic tensions in U.S.-Japan relations between the onset of the Second Sino-Japanese War and the outbreak of the Pacific War. The July 1938 Hawkins memorandum is particularly significant as an unvarnished internal policy debate revealing the State Department's calculation that terminating the 1911 commercial treaty would incur minimal economic retaliation, while candidly acknowledging that the U.S. had itself manipulated tariff classifications and value brackets to exclude Japanese goods in potential violation of the treaty's spirit. Furthermore, the 1940–1941 consular despatches illuminate the micro-level friction over wartime municipal taxation and diplomatic privileges in Japan, showing how local fiscal pressures led Japanese municipalities to introduce rental-based 'Citizens' Taxes' to replace abolished surcharges, while consular officials carefully parsed the boundaries of bilateral reciprocal shipping tax agreements and official diplomatic immunity.
keywords: Treaty of Commerce and Navigation of 1911
overview: This file (State Department decimal file 894.512, covering Japanese financial conditions and taxation) spans July 1938 to April 1941 and documents U.S.-Japanese diplomatic and consular interactions concerning bilateral commercial treaties and Japanese taxation policies affecting American interests. The bundle begins with a July 1938 Department of State memorandum by Harry C. Hawkins examining the commercial and legal ramifications of terminating the 1911 Treaty of Commerce and Navigation with Japan, advising against alleging Japanese treaty violations due to potential counter-accusations regarding American tariff specialization. It also contains a March 1940 cross-reference sheet regarding Ambassador Joseph C. Grew's refutation of allegations that Tokyo Embassy officers abused diplomatic duty-free privileges by reselling American automobiles subject to a Japanese sales tax. Finally, the file includes January 1941 despatches from American Consul Samuel Sokobin in Kobe reporting on municipal assessments under the newly instituted local 'Citizens' Tax,' detailing the successful exemption of U.S. Treasury representative Mr. Daley on grounds of official status and analyzing whether American shipping firms, specifically the States Steamship Company, could claim reciprocal exemption from the municipal rental-based levy under the 1924 reciprocal shipping tax waiver.

subfiles.about: Analyzes the commercial, legal, and political implications of terminating the 1911 Treaty of Commerce and Navigation with Japan, advising on negotiation strategy, retaliatory risks, and grounds for termination.
keywords: Treaty of Commerce and Navigation of 1911
subfiles.summary: Harry C. Hawkins of the Division of Trade Agreements assesses the potential consequences of terminating the 1911 Treaty of Commerce and Navigation with Japan. He concludes that Japanese retaliatory measures would have minimal immediate effect because Japan had already restricted imports to essentials, but warns that termination would remove protections against Japanese bilateralism and prejudice future trade development. Hawkins strongly advises against justifying termination on grounds of Japanese treaty violations, noting that Japan could retaliate by accusing the United States of violating the treaty through tariff specialization and value brackets. Instead, he recommends either seeking revision to modernize provisions and introduce neutrality safeguards (citing the Italian and Czechoslovak precedents) or terminating without explanation.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Harry C. Hawkins to the Secretary of State regarding proposed termination of the 1911 commercial treaty with Japan

subfiles.about: Indexes Ambassador Grew's despatch rebutting allegations that Tokyo diplomatic officers abused duty-free privileges by importing and reselling American automobiles subject to Japanese sales tax.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference sheet refers to Despatch No. 4594 of March 15, 1940, from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew in Tokyo (filed under 694.11241/41). The despatch takes issue with a report from the Consul at Yokohama (Despatch No. 635) asserting that Tokyo diplomatic officers routinely imported American cars duty-free and resold them at substantial profits, prompting the Japanese government to impose a 40% sales tax on such vehicles. Grew strongly objected to the implication that Embassy officers had engaged in transactions constituting an abuse of diplomatic privileges.
subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 4594 regarding Foreign Service officers' automobiles and Japanese sales tax

subfiles.about: Reports that the Kobe municipal Citizens' Tax assessment against U.S. Treasury representative Mr. Daley was rescinded as an error due to his official position.
subfiles.summary: American Consul Samuel Sokobin reports to Ambassador Joseph C. Grew regarding an assessment of 31.75 yen levied as 'Citizens' Tax' on U.S. Treasury Representative Mr. Daley in Kobe. Following an informal inquiry by Mr. Daley at the Kobe municipal office, local authorities admitted that the tax notification had been sent in error and confirmed that no claim would be made against him due to his official standing. Sokobin notes that no other consular officers received tax notices, indicating that municipal authorities intend to exempt American consular officers and official employees from the tax. The subfile includes the filed copy and two certified true copies of the despatch.
subfiles.title: Despatch from Consul Samuel Sokobin to Ambassador Joseph C. Grew regarding assessment of Citizens' Tax on U.S. Treasury representative at Kobe

subfiles.about: Examines whether American shipping firms, particularly States Steamship Company, are liable for the newly enacted Kobe municipal Citizens' Tax despite reciprocal shipping tax exemptions.
subfiles.summary: Consul Samuel Sokobin forwards an inquiry from the States Steamship Company regarding an assessment of 74.30 yen in municipal 'Citizens' Tax,' calculated on its monthly office rental in Kobe. The shipping company argued it was exempt under the reciprocal 1924 Japanese-American arrangement waiving income taxes on shipping earnings, contending the levy was a substitute for the abolished municipal income tax surcharge. Sokobin analyzes Japanese laws and prior State Department instructions from 1928, concluding that reciprocal tax exemptions applied only to national income taxes on vessel earnings rather than municipal levies or local office rentals, though he submits the matter to Ambassador Grew for study. The document includes detailed municipal tax rate tables and calculations for corporate and individual renters, along with duplicate carbon copies of the despatch and enclosures.
subfiles.title: Despatch from Consul Samuel Sokobin to Ambassador Joseph C. Grew regarding applicability of Kobe Citizens' Tax to American shipping companies, with enclosures
